piezas.titulo: 'I Just Wanted It to End': Sensory Experiences of Autistic Women During Pregnancy and Childbirth.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Autistic women experience the perinatal cycle with specific sensory challenges that remain insufficiently documented, particularly among those with diverse support levels. This qualitative study investigated sensory processing experiences of autistic women during pregnancy and labour, and how environmental and attitudinal factors articulate with sensory overload. Thirty-four autistic Brazilian women with Support Levels 1 and 2 ( Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders [5th ed., text rev.]) participated in four Hermeneutic-Dialectic Circle (HDC) cycles through semi-structured interviews in multiple formats. Iterative hermeneutic-dialectic analysis, supported by NVivo, identified four themes: (1) Pregnancy as a sensory amplifier; (2) The birth environment as the epicentre of sensory overload; (3) Communication barriers and professional invalidation; and (4) Sensory experiences in early motherhood. Pregnancy amplified pre-existing sensitivities, particularly olfactory and proprioceptive. The hospital environment emerged as the epicentre of overload, with touch as the most aversive stimulus. Peritraumatic dissociation was reported by 19 participants (56%). The deliberate inclusion of women with intellectual disability and complex communication needs revealed that saturation observed in earlier cycles was artifactual, a finding with methodological implications for qualitative autism research.Lay AbstractAutistic women often face challenges during pregnancy, childbirth and the postpartum period related to how they process sensory information such as sounds, lights, touch and smells. Very little research has explored how these differences affect the experience of becoming a mother, and even less has included autistic women with higher support needs or complex communication needs. This study explored the sensory experiences of 34 autistic women in Brazil through in-depth interviews, deliberately including women with Support Levels 1 and 2, some of whom used augmentative and alternative communication. The interviews were conducted in multiple formats (video call, in-person and text messaging) to ensure accessibility. We found that pregnancy amplified pre-existing sensory sensitivities. Smells, temperature changes and foetal movement were experienced with an intensity far beyond what is typically reported, sometimes causing shutdowns and crises. The hospital birth environment was a major source of sensory overload, with touch being the most distressing stimulus: 31 of 34 women reported aversive experiences related to being touched during labour. Even comfort techniques widely recommended for pain relief, such as massage, were described as unbearable. Communication barriers intensified suffering throughout the perinatal cycle: women reported that health care professionals frequently dismissed their sensory experiences as exaggeration or anxiety, which made it harder to access appropriate care. More than half the participants (19 of 34) reported memory gaps and dissociation during labour, suggesting that childbirth can be a traumatic event for autistic women when care is not adapted to their sensory needs. When health care teams made accommodations (reducing lighting, minimising unnecessary touch, maintaining continuity of care, providing predictability), women reported substantially better experiences. A key methodological finding was that the apparent saturation of themes observed when only women with Support Level 1 were interviewed proved artifactual: including women with higher support needs revealed new and important experiences that would otherwise have been missed. These findings highlight the need for sensory-informed, neurodiversity-affirming perinatal care and for research that deliberately includes autistic women with diverse support levels and communication profiles.

piezas.titulo: Validity and Reliability of the Activity Card Sort 3 in Persons With Thumb Carpometacarpal Osteoarthritis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceAlthough individuals with thumb carpometacarpal (CMC1) osteoarthritis (OA) commonly experience participation restrictions, participation-focused outcome measures remain underinvestigated, and clinicians primarily rely on assessments of impairments in body structures and functions.ObjectiveTo determine the concurrent validity, test-retest reliability, and precision of the Activity Card Sort 3 (ACS3) in individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA.DesignSingle-cohort observational psychometric study with repeated measures over a 2-week interval.SettingRemote assessments conducted via videoconferencing.ParticipantsThirty-three adults with radiographically confirmed CMC1 OA completed two virtual assessments approximately 2 weeks apart.Outcomes and MeasuresConcurrent validity was examined by comparing ACS3 domain and total scores with the World Health Organization Disability Assessment Schedule 2.0 (WHODAS 2.0). Test-retest reliability of the "current," "previous," and "% retained" activities scores was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC 3,1 ). Precision was assessed using the standard error of measurement and minimal detectable change.ResultsThe ACS3 demonstrated good concurrent validity through strong associations with conceptually related WHODAS 2.0 domains. "Current" and "% retained" scores demonstrated good-to-excellent test-retest reliability across all domains. "Current" scores consistently showed the highest reliability and precision. "Previous" scores demonstrated lower reliability and greater measurement error, suggesting recall bias. Carrying forward "previous" scores from session 1 to session 2 improved the reliability of "% retained" scores.Conclusions and RelevanceThe ACS3 is a valid and reliable measure of participation for individuals with nonoperative CMC1 OA. The "current" and "% retained" scores may support occupational therapy practitioners in conducting participation-focused assessment of persons with CMC1 OA.

piezas.titulo: I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened
piezas.resumenOriginal: Science has a spam problem. And the spam filter is getting clogged up. According to all reports, academic publishing is drowning in what has come to be called AI slop: low-quality, mass-produced content generated with AI. By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023. What’s more, over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025. Given that for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it , these figures likely grossly underestimate LLM involvement today. Of course, evidence of AI use doesn’t necessarily mean a paper is slop. But some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually. “It’s not just the [scientific] record under threat, it’s science as a whole,” warns Amanda Sulicz , IEEE’s research-integrity manager. “AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.” Yet statistics and statements claiming that the problem is big—perhaps even existential for science—don’t really get the message across. Just how easy is it to use AI to create a convincing but completely fake paper? And without adding even more to the burden on stretched peer reviewers, who do this work on a volunteer basis, do publishers have the tools to keep AI slop out of the scientific record? Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney , managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access , if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed. The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research? Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system. Round 1: Creating the Forgery To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone. I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape. My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious. I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access ’s required style. At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed. What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.” Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too. Round 1: Attempt to Publish Two Ways to Make a Paper With AI I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself. ROUND 1: CHATGPT + GEMINI 1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field. 2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections. 3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.” 4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access . 5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access , where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. → CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references. ROUND 2: FARS 1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes. 2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal. 3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete. 4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article. 5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access . → CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints. Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job? As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini! In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub , she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong ” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.” Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto , an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable. The AI Arms Race On one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making. These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi , IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through. Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics. Burden on Academics Mahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop. Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. What Gave Away My AI Papers Round 1: The Fake Paper Created with free versions of ChatGPT and Gemini Ghost citations Many references were fabricated or couldn’t be validated. Questionable scientific claims An expert flagged confidently stated claims that were at best debatable. Too many acronyms The expert also noted excessive use of acronyms in the abstract. Round 2: The AI-Research Paper Created by the autonomous research system FARS Too many preprints The references were real, but too many pointed to non-peer-reviewed preprints. Nonsense in a figure One technical figure contained a line labeled “lhewl.” AI artifacts Another figure’s depiction of an AI “brain” contained telltale random dots. There are two high-profile homes for this important and completely volunteer-led post-publication review work. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record. Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky , cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles. Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.” Blurred Lines My homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System) , AutoResearchClaw , The AIScientist-v2 , Zochi , AI Researcher , and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw , for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery. The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.” FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours , was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma . “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su , Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.) Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test. Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine FARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously. Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time. With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours. At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney. Round 2: Attempt to Publish Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one. “Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem. In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated. Automation Changing the Landscape Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process. “FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge ,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.” In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?” A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future? Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.” In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?” To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’” Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent. Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud. See the AI-Generated Papers Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication. Paper 1: The AI-Generated Forgery Created with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened. Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research Paper Created with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI. Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

piezas.titulo: 2023 Community Workshop: Let's Talk Sense
piezas.resumenOriginal: 2023 Community Workshop: Let's Talk Sense STAR Admin Fri, 02/17/2023 - 20:50 Join STAR Institute and some of its expert clinicians for three nights of learning as we explore the keys to a sensory-informed life. Each night, STAR's Clinical Director will be joined by a different STAR therapist to share tips and strategies around some of families' most often asked questions including: “How can I support and be there for my family when I am constantly feeling burned out?” “What can I do to help my child transition from thing to thing/place to place more smoothly?" “We feel like we walk on egg shells around our child. Why is that and what can we do?" Each night will begin with a 30-40 minute conversation led by the therapist before a live Q&A where you can ask STAR’s occupational therapists and mental health providers your own questions. piezas.titulo: Agent Factory recap: Agent harnesses, shifting left, and autonomous coding
piezas.resumenOriginal: In this episode of The Agent Factory , we explore the reality of building with autonomous agents alongside Ryan Lopopolo, a software engineer at Google Cloud and the person who coined the term agent harness . From throwing out manual code editors to treating team collaboration like leveling up RPG stats, Ryan breaks down how grounding models in rich context and shifting interventions left unlocks high levels of agent autonomy. This post guides you through the key ideas from our conversation. Use it to quickly recap topics or dive deeper into specific segments with links and timestamps. The Agent Harness - What is it? Timestamp: [ 00:30 ] An AI agent as we're defining it here is a large language model (LLM) plus an agent harness . Think of the harness as everything wrapped around the LLM that isn't the model itself. For example, if you're working in Google Antigravity using Gemini 3.8 Flash , Gemini Flash is the LLM and Google Antigravity is the harness. While an unassisted model can answer simple questions out of the box, it can't check live conditions or interact with your workspace on its own. When a user asks a question like "Why is the sky blue?" , an unassisted LLM can respond without issue. However, when asked a question like "Should I wear a raincoat today?" , the model can't answer on its own because it lacks the necessary data. The harness catches the intent, queries live weather tools, bundles that context back into the prompt, and hands it to the model to produce an informed answer. Ryan Lopopolo on agent harnesses and autonomous coding Tilde Thurium sat down with Ryan Lopopolo to discuss what it takes to run fully autonomous coding workflows in production. See the summary below! Coining the harness and writing zero production code Timestamp: [ 02:22 ] The term agent harness grew out of Ryan's extensive work on autonomous coding agents, culminating in a February 2026 essay on leveraging coding models in an agent-first world. Ryan shared that he hasn't opened a traditional code editor since May of last year, maintaining that streak through his transition into Google Cloud . In this paradigm, engineers no longer author or review individual lines of syntax; instead, they operate at the level of natural language specifications and inspect the final artifacts, such as pull requests, documents, and spreadsheets. Then they determine whether the end result meets organizational standards. Harness engineering is the study and the practice of putting a model into an environment where it can succeed. If you don't do that work, you end up doing what I call 'prompt and pray'. Ryan Lopopolo Context curation and lazy prompting Timestamp: [ 03:35 ] Upfront harness investment pays off by allowing engineers to become lazy prompters. When the repository contains structured documentation, clear interfaces, and discoverable tools, you do not need to paste walls of text into a prompt box every morning "I aspire to be an incredibly lazy prompter. If I have done the job to give the model the tools and context it needs to ground itself, I don't need to write a long prompt. It figures it out." The model uses its harness to pull relevant context, allowing it to navigate large codebases and execute complex tasks without oversight. Shifting left: engineering best practices as autonomous guardrails Timestamp: [ 05:00 ] When an agent fails, developers face a whole spectrum of interventions. The most common reflex is to fiddle with the prompt or retry, but that never scales across a team. "The simplest, smooth-brain, stupidest intervention I can think of is literally just: try my prompt again without changing anything else. But shifting left means moving interventions earlier into the development lifecycle where they are cheapest and automated: from prompts, to repo docs, to linters, to tests, and all the way to upstream evals." Instead of hoping the model guesses right on the next turn, shifting left embeds standards directly into the environment. Linters, tests, and AGENTS.md files act as durable memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, making sure the agent stays on the rails without needing constant hand-holding. Leveraging established tools and determinism Timestamp: [ 06:50 ] Agents shine when they're handed tools that already mirror patterns heavily represented in pre-training data. Pairing models with standard command-line interfaces moves reasoning into determinism, shifting the burden of context aggregation away from the model and onto reliable tools. Ryan also shared an environmental design trick for context efficiency: structuring markdown files so link anchors sit directly beneath their corresponding prose blocks rather than inline. This prevents context clutter and mitigates "lost in the middle" retrieval issues. Because Ryan operates exclusively by reviewing end-state artifacts, keeping documentation readable allows him to easily inspect execution runs: "I want to be able to look at the pull request and review it. If it made a bad decision, I need to know where it went off the rails so I can whack the agent on the head and make sure it does not make that same mistake again." Long horizons and expanding the agentic loop Timestamp: [ 09:45 ] The central challenge of harness engineering is ensuring that agents cohere over long time horizons. Because human organizations produce software through iterative refinement rather than single-shot prompts, agent workflows must mirror that cadence. Harness engineering uses tightly scoped, reviewable pull requests to narrow the agent's state space. Stacking these high-confidence changes end-to-end allows supervisors to gradually expand the loop size, building trust until agents can autonomously execute large-scale initiatives, including entire language migrations Curating agent teams like RPG stats Timestamp: [ 11:58 ] Rather than divvying up sprint tasks based on individual specialties, having a diverse team contribute to an agent turns it into a central producer of work that carries everyone's strengths. Ryan compared leveling up an agent's capabilities to building out a character sheet: "[It's like] building out the stats of your RPG character. I get a new person on the team who is a React architect and boom! The attention that they pay is able to bump out the stats in front-end architecture and performance." With that collective expertise baked into the environment, the agent can autonomously classify incoming work and activate the exact skills it needs on demand, operating as both a backend architect and a front-end specialist. Accruing leverage in tools, not custom harnesses Timestamp: [ 14:38 ] For developers wondering whether to build their own custom agent harness, Ryan offered clear advice: don't build one from scratch. Standard harnesses already provide the foundational primitives: file reading, grep search, and command execution. Over-scaffolding an agent with rigid, bespoke frameworks creates technical debt and leads to sunk-cost traps when frontier models advance. "If you focus all of your efforts on improving quality on tools and context, you can freely adopt the newest models as they come out and you'll be constantly accruing leverage into a bit of the system that will never become obsolete." Operating Google Cloud and eliminating capability overhang Timestamp: [ 16:47 ] Discussing his work at Google Cloud , Ryan outlined his motivation to eliminate capability overhang : the delta between what frontier AI models are theoretically capable of and how much useful work is currently extracted in production. Because the cloud functions as a massive, programmable surface, equipping agents with direct interfaces to Google Cloud lets them manage and deploy infrastructure effectively, turning raw model capability into tangible enterprise utility. Continually updating your priors on AI Timestamp: [ 18:13 ] The speed of AI development requires engineers and teams to actively unlearn old limitations and constantly reassess what these models can achieve. " It's very important to continually be updating what you think is possible with these lovely tools that we have ," Ryan urged. What broke six months ago often runs effortlessly on today's frontier models. Rather than getting locked into rigid workflows, developers should build around the two highly extensible interfaces that will remain relevant across every model upgrade: tools and context. "Agents will always need context in order to do that last mile adaptation into what you think good is. And as you can continue to... shift it to the left, in terms of increasingly capable tools which act as a form of memory and enforcement of what you think good looks like, you'll continually be amazed as the models are able to do more and more interesting things for you over time." How To Build A Custom Harness Next, Billy Jacobson started us off by showing how developers can customize their own agent harnesses for specific tasks. Under the hood: Why build a custom harness? Timestamp: [ 19:44 ] Before jumping into code, Billy unpacked why developers should understand the mechanics of a harness rather than treating it like a black box. Recalling advice from an engineering mentor that "You can just use the framework, but a great engineer will really understand the framework" , Billy explained that building a harness yourself is the best way to debug what happens when an agent breaks. You can evaluate three core design decisions for every workflow: Looping : How many iterations should the agent run, and what conditions trigger an exit state? Tools : What specific tools should the agent access, and when and how should it invoke them? Memory : How important is conversational and operational memory, and when should it be retrieved or compacted? Linear Agent Harness: Deterministic Single-Pass Execution Timestamp: [ 21:34 ] Billy demonstrated a minimalist linear harness designed for deterministic workflows where looping is unnecessary. This pattern is ideal for targeted inspections, file transformations, or single-turn data analyses where you want a high level of determinism and need the agent to perform the exact same execution flow every single time. Closed-Loop Agent Harness: Iterative Test-Driven Repair Timestamp: [ 22:45 ] When tasks demand active bug fixing and refactoring, a closed-loop harness provides the iterative reasoning required to reach a verified resolution. In this demo, Billy showcased an agent that applies an automated code edit to address a failing requirement, and the harness executes the unit test suite against the updated codebase. If the tests fail, the runtime captures standard failure logs and detailed stack traces, feeding those error diagnostics directly back into the agent's working memory. The process repeats continuously until all unit tests pass, backed by a five-iteration ceiling to prevent infinite loops and runaway execution costs. Guardrail Harness with Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) Timestamp: [ 23:25 ] For developers who require custom behavior without rewriting core orchestration plumbing from scratch, Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK) provides scaffolding with automated memory management and execution safeguards. Billy walked through an example that leverages ADK's native context compaction to summarize older conversational turns, preventing context window bloat during extended debugging runs. Custom interception hooks inspect and filter shell actions before execution, automatically stopping high-risk operations such as recursive file deletions, database drops, or unauthorized remote git pushes. This architecture gives teams fine-grained control over tool execution boundaries while avoiding the maintenance burden of bespoke harness frameworks. The 3-Layer Agent Dev Stack: Gemini 3.8 Flash, Google Antigravity, and Google Skills Timestamp: [ 25:27 ] Next up, Smitha Kolan broke down why coding agents do not always require heavier reasoning models, emphasizing that high performance stems from balancing the three layers of the agent stack: Model , Harness , and Knowledge . "Your coding agent doesn't need a smarter model. It needs a better stack: model, harness, and knowledge. When all three click into place, everything changes." She then walked through the three tools she's been loving recently, one for each layer of the stack. Layer 1 | Model | Gemini 3.8 Flash : High-frequency agentic loops run between 20 and 60 sequential hops per task (inspecting files, updating functions, and executing unit tests). Because latency and API costs compound across iterations, a lightweight, responsive model like Gemini 3.8 Flash makes real-time agent loops practical without running up a massive bill. Layer 2 | Harness | Google Antigravity with /boost : Default Antigravity handles standard navigation and component creation. On top of that, the /boost command spins up an orchestrator that coordinates specialized sub-agents in parallel and concludes with an independent audit pass before modifying files. Layer 3 | Knowledge | Google Skills Repository : With over 19,000 GitHub stars and 100+ curated domain packages across Google Cloud, Firebase, Flutter, and Maps, this harness-agnostic repository injects precise domain context on demand, preventing agents from guessing cloud configurations Your turn to build Building effective coding agents requires moving past the reflex of simply swapping in larger models. As Ryan Lopopolo's philosophy of harness engineering illustrates, true developer leverage is achieved by shifting best practices to the left and investing in rich tools, deterministic verifiers, and well-curated context that survive model upgrades. When combined with fast inference models, structured orchestration harnesses, and modular domain knowledge, agents evolve from conversational novelties into dependable, autonomous engineering partners. Ready to put it into practice? Explore the tools and resources covered in this episode: Gemini 3.8 Flash : Fast, low-cost model for multi-hop agent loops. Google Antigravity ( /boost ): Orchestrator harness for parallel coding agents and verification. Google Skills : Modular domain knowledge for Google Cloud, Firebase, and Flutter. Agent Development Kit (ADK) : Custom harness middleware for safety guardrails and memory compaction. Full episode video : The full interview and live Factory Floor code demos. piezas.resumenOriginal: GitHub Octoverse 2026 I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular: This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month. The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this: Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location . Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...] Industry . Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...] Interoperability . Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation. piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 21
piezas.resumenOriginal: Gergely Orosz is frustrated at those that entered his explicitly “No AI” essay competition and used AI. He goes on to say: When I start to suspect some part is AI about someone I don’t know: how can I tell how much of it is? And how much time and effort do I want to invest to figure out? I fear most people do not realize this last part: that when it takes time and effort from others to figure out what % is AI, and what % is YOU, then I will simply assume it’s probably 100% AI and 0% you So when producing anything that is meant for other humans, if you use even a little AI, you risk the assumption that it is all AI and pointless to pay attention to In general, I agree with him, and react much the same. Once I hear LLM Voice, I flip the bozo bit and check out of the post. But as I do this I have caveats. How accurate is my neural net at AI-detection, are humans taking on AI-ish elements in their normal communication? And more seriously there are some valid uses for AI. Jim Highsmith’s story of his second brain helping him deal with Parkinson’s is one. Another is folks who don’t know English well, using AI to translate. Am I being unfair when I flip the AI voice bit when I read/listen to them? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I was sad to hear that the Grace Hopper Celebration is canceled this year. It’s an event run by Anitab.org to promote women and non-binary technologists in the software industry. Many of my colleagues have been encouraged and inspired by going to this event, which makes a refreshing change to what is often a male-dominated world. It seems the current crusade against diversity initiatives has had a big impact on funding. We are still a long way from where we should be on gender diversity in our profession, and losing an event like this only makes things more difficult. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ I’ve always found Cindy Sridharan’s writing to be worth reading, and she’s broken a quiet period with a monster of an article: How to effectively debug when you no longer understand the code . Since Medium estimates it as a 64 minute read, I didn’t jump in lightly, but settled down on a flight from Amsterdam to Stuttgart. I’m glad I did, because there’s lot of good material in there, and I’d struggle to find anything to cut. In the article she uses three recent bug hunts to surface principles for how to best use an AI tool for debugging. Much of this is governed by this wise observation: Agents are not humans. They’re far more capable than humans when it comes to many things, and we should be leaning into these strengths, rather than trying to get agents to replicate human patterns of problem solving which might be suboptimal in agentic contexts. One conclusion from her experiences is that the code often isn’t the best thing for agents to look at having an agent start an investigation by first reading the code is an anti-pattern. In fact, reading the code first to formulate hypotheses about a bug should always be the very last resort of the agentic investigation process, not the starting point. An agent should first collect all available evidence about the bug, and only then formulate the hypotheses from the code that might best explain what’s being observed. She distinguishes between a bottom tier of facts: raw data that agent can find about the behavior of the system - and an upper tier of hypotheses: inferences that the agents make based on that data. Diagnosing a bug now becomes a problem of finding the hypothesis in the top tier that satisfies every fact from the bottom tier. The agents need to be steered towards the hypotheses that are the likest cause of the bug and then subject these hypotheses to validation. She has a three-step process to do this. First she identifies the most important facts, the signals that might explain or identify the bug. The factual tier has many data points. Not all of them are equally valuable. In fact, some of it might be active noise that doesn’t help an agent to be steered towards most promising hypothesis. The agent first needs to identify the data points in the factual tier that are actually related to the bug. Agents do this best when they are given a high-quality control A control is a behavior of the system that doesn’t exhibit the bug. This may be requests that trigger the bug compared to those that don’t, or different builds of the product, or the same build in different environments. With signals highlighted, she then focuses on the hypotheses that are most promising, because they fit best with the signals. A hypothesis should satisfy all the facts, the most valuable signals are those that are only satisfied by a few hypotheses. A table of hypotheses and signals helps visualize the strength of the signals and the likelihood of the hypotheses. The third step is then validating the promising hypotheses against every fact, treating each fact as constraint on the solution. Across the three bugs chronicled in this post, my most valuable contributions weren’t knowledge of the code. They were picking a control, choosing a constraint, and rejecting a hypothesis that hadn’t been validated. The engineers who thrive in an agent-native world will be the ones who are good at designing such verification loops, whether or not they understand the code it verifies. This directing has to remember the opening point that agents have different capabilities to humans. A human wants to deal with less data. All abstractions we currently have (aggregation, visualizations etc) are designed to help humans deal with less data. An agent, however, needs more raw data; its strength lies in processing huge volumes of data at a rapid clip. Aggregation — the thing that makes a dashboard useful to a human — is often the thing that destroys the value of the signal for an agent Agents’ ability to consume lots of raw data also affects how we build systems. More logging gives agents more data to chew on. And thus far, the human is still necessary to direct the agent In each of the three bugs chronicled in this post, the agent was more than capable of getting to the root cause by itself, but it didn’t do so. It didn’t set up a control in the “latency bug” until I asked it to While it’s a long post, it’s engagingly written and full of useful details. I hope my little summary encourages you to give it the read it deserves.

piezas.titulo: ScyllaDB in Enterprise Java: High-Performance NoSQL With Eclipse JNoSQL
piezas.resumenOriginal: Modern enterprise applications must process increasing data volumes while guaranteeing low latency, high availability, and predictable performance. While relational databases are essential for transactional workloads and complex queries, some applications do not fit the relational model. Systems that manage millions of user engagements, financial events, or IoT data often need a persistence solution built for distributed environments and horizontal scalability. In these cases, ScyllaDB affords a compelling option for enterprise architects. ScyllaDB is a high-performance, distributed NoSQL database based on the wide-column data model. Inspired by Apache Cassandra and compatible with its query language (CQL), ScyllaDB uses a shard-per-core architecture to maximize hardware efficiency and preserve consistent performance under intensive workloads. When should ScyllaDB be chosen over traditional relational databases or other NoSQL options? This article examines its column-family model, compares it with Cassandra, and shows how to integrate ScyllaDB into a Java enterprise application.

piezas.titulo: Resolving the apparent paradox of multisensory expertise: coupling priors, common-cause priors, and how to distinguish among them
piezas.resumenOriginal: Perceptual expertise is widely assumed to refine multisensory perception, yet the empirical literature appears inconsistent. Trained musicians show narrower audiovisual temporal integration windows and quicker segregation, whereas experienced wine tasters seem more influenced by a wine's color in their aroma and flavor judgments than novices are. We argue that the inconsistency arises from a conflation of two formally distinct quantities: the prior probability that concurrent signals arise from a common source, and the coupling between the values of signals that share one. We present a generative model in which both are free parameters, along with channel precision and a decision criterion, that contains causal-inference and coupling-prior models as special cases. The model shows that the correlation between the values of two signals across an environment reflects only the product of the two priors, so that a correlation-tracking learner acquires the coupling when the signals always share a source, whereas separating the two priors requires representing causal structure; that binary common-source reports confound the common-cause prior with the decision criterion; that the coupling trades off against the measurement noise of the influencing channel unless its precision is measured independently; and that the two priors leave distinct signatures in how cross-modal influence varies with disparity. When the source is fixed, as for the color and odor of a wine, tighter coupling alone produces the conjunction of greater displacement by color and better discrimination between wines reported for experienced tasters, which no change in odor precision can produce. Simulations of a test battery combining continuous estimates, common-source reports and discrimination thresholds show that the parameters can be recovered, that a within-subject dissociation can be detected with conventional sample sizes under illustrative effect sizes, and that recovery fails in certain cases. The account yields a rule classifying environments by their base rate of common causation and their coupling strength, and the same ambiguity attends claims about altered multisensory processing in autism and aging. We also show that the most cited demonstration of expert susceptibility to color contains no expertise manipulation, and suggest that apparent expert biases may reflectwind calibration to real-world statistics.

piezas.titulo: Effects of acceptance and commitment therapy on psychological and health-related outcomes in stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundStroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide and is frequently accompanied by psychological and functional impairments. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a third-wave behavioral intervention focusing on psychological flexibility, has been increasingly applied in stroke rehabilitation. Although previous reviews have suggested beneficial effects of ACT in stroke patients, whether these benefits persist in the short term after the intervention ends, and the certainty of the evidence, remain unclear.MethodsA systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261325108). Randomized controlled trials evaluating ACT in stroke patients were included. Pooled effects were calculated using random-effects models, with separate analyses for post-intervention and follow-up outcomes. Sources of heterogeneity were explored using subgroup analyses and meta-regression. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework.ResultsTwenty-two RCTs involving 1,975 participants were included. ACT may be associated with reductions in depressive symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = −1.32, 95% CI: −1.80 to −0.84; follow-up: SMD = −0.76, 95% CI: −1.07 to −0.45) and anxiety symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = −1.36, 95% CI: −1.90 to −0.82; follow-up: SMD = −0.51, 95% CI: −1.42 to 0.40, not significant); depressive symptoms remained statistically significant at follow-up. Heterogeneity was considerable for both outcomes at post-intervention (I2 = 93.68% for depression and 93.60% for anxiety), so the pooled estimates represent average effects across studies. ACT may also be associated with improvements in psychological flexibility, quality of life, and sleep quality; however, these outcomes were based on a limited number of studies and showed considerable heterogeneity (I2 = 74.68 to 92.26%), so they should be interpreted cautiously. However, no statistically significant effects were observed for activities of daily living, neurological function, or hope. ACT did not appear to increase dropout rates in the available studies (K = 16; RR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.58–1.69). Meta-regression analyses indicated that intervention duration may not be a significant moderator of treatment effects. The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, mainly due to risk of bias and inconsistency.ConclusionAcceptance and Commitment Therapy may be a useful adjunctive intervention for improving psychological outcomes in people with stroke. However, evidence for functional recovery remains insufficient. Future high-quality RCTs with standardized protocols, larger samples, and longer follow-up are needed to confirm the long-term effectiveness of ACT.Systematic review registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifer CRD420261325108.

piezas.titulo: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas
piezas.resumenOriginal: El malestar psicológico a través del inglés y otros idiomas emcamara 29/10/2026 26/11/2026 Fecha y hora: 26/11/26, 5pm CET Ponentes : Anna-Maria Bucur, Dalle Molle Institute for Artificial Intelligence, Università della Svizzera italiana Presentador: Por confirmar. Resumen: La presentación analiza cómo el procesamiento del lenguaje natural puede respaldar la investigación psicológica analizando interacciones procedentes de redes sociales para comprender mejor el malestar psicológico. Mientras que el PLN resulta eficaz a la hora de identificar patrones lingüísticos, la psicología articula la investigación definiendo los conceptos clave, explicando su relevancia y aportando un marco para interpretar los hallazgos. La ponencia comienza con varios estudios de caso centrados en la supervivencia al cáncer, la identificación de problemas de salud mental en la población general y la exploración de momentos de felicidad en personas diagnosticadas con depresión, todos ellos a partir de datos en inglés. A continuación, aborda consideraciones transculturales al trabajar con datos en idiomas distintos del inglés y evalúa los modelos del lenguaje de gran tamaño (LLM) para este fin. La presentación subraya que un PLN fundamentado en la teoría puede desvelar trayectorias psicológicas y ofrecer perspectivas valiosas para las intervenciones terapéuticas. No obstante, también destaca cómo la falta de datos de calidad y de evaluaciones adecuadas plantea retos a la hora de desarrollar métodos aplicables a lenguas más allá del inglés. Reseña: Ana-Maria Bucur es investigadora postdoctoral en el Instituto Dalle Molle de Inteligencia Artificial (IDSIA), Università della Svizzera italiana, donde trabaja en el Laboratorio de Recuperación de Información del profesor Fabio Crestani. Realizó un doctorado en cotutela entre la Universitat Politècnica de València y la Universidad de Bucarest, bajo la dirección de los profesores Paolo Rosso y Liviu P. Dinu. Ana-Maria ha participado en colaboraciones interdisciplinares que abarcan tanto la psicología como las humanidades digitales. Su investigación se centra principalmente en el procesamiento del lenguaje natural (PLN) aplicado a la salud mental, investigando en especial cómo las personas expresan sus estados psicológicos a través del lenguaje y de qué manera los métodos computacionales pueden mejorar nuestra comprensión de la salud mental y respaldar el bienestar. Más recientemente, ha estado explorando cómo influye la cultura en las manifestaciones de los trastornos mentales y cómo desarrollar métodos computacionales con sensibilidad cultural para un cribado de salud mental más inclusivo. piezas.titulo: An information-theoretic analysis of the tsetse fly (Glossina morsitans) antenna reveals trichoid sensilla as the main carriers of odor identity
piezas.resumenOriginal: Tsetse flies locate vertebrate hosts largely by smell, and odor-baited devices are central to tsetse and trypanosomiasis control. A published electrophysiological survey of the Glossina morsitans antenna defined seven classes of olfactory sensilla, but descriptive clustering cannot reveal how much information these classes carry or which odors they distinguish. We reanalyzed responses of 182 sensilla to 16-17 odorants using Fisher-Rao information geometry, bias-corrected mutual information, Bayesian decoding, and signal detection theory. In the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, trichoid sensilla are largely dedicated to pheromones. In tsetse, the three trichoid classes carried more information about odor identity than the four basiconic classes (1.92 vs. 1.14 bits, of a possible 4), a difference of 0.78 bits (95% confidence interval 0.44-1.10), and were strongly excited by the host attractant 1-octen-3-ol. Adding trichoid to basiconic sensilla raised decoding accuracy from 32% to 70% (23% to 55% for decoders tested on held-out sensilla) and identified 1-octen-3-ol on 98% of trials (92% held out). The basiconic code was nearly one-dimensional (participation ratio 1.71), organized along an axis of response strength with 1-octen-3-ol at its extreme. The CO2-sensitive ab4 class was the most sensitive detector for 11 of 16 odorants, whereas ab2 carried no detectable odor information. Classes shared up to 0.41 bits of their information with one another, an overlap only weakly predicted by the similarity of their mean tuning. On a shared odor panel, Drosophila receptors carried twice the information per channel and, with channel number matched, spanned about 1.5-fold more dimensions. These conclusions held in simulations at the real sample sizes, under alternative noise models, and when classes were defined on independent odorants. The tsetse antenna thus combines redundant, detection-oriented basiconic channels with trichoid sensilla that carry host-odor identity, principles relevant to the design of odor baits.

piezas.titulo: Individual Differences in Perceived Complexity, Visual Discomfort, and Preference for Images Varying in Spectral Scaling.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Participants ( N = 89) rated preference, discomfort, and perceived complexity of grayscale, thresholded, edge and mountain profile images varying in spectral scaling properties. Participants also completed self-report questionnaires designed to measure neurodivergent (CATI, ASRS) or sensory processing sensitivity (CHYPS-V, SPQ-S). Across image types, perceived complexity and discomfort declined as the spectral slope parameter increased, whereas preference increased from the shallowest to the intermediate slopes and then plateaued. Self-reported autistic-like traits, ADHD-like traits, and sensory sensitivity were largely unrelated to overall rating levels but showed small associations with how ratings changed across spectral slope. These findings support treating complexity, discomfort, and preference as related but non-equivalent visual judgments, with trait-related influences expressed mainly as modest variation in sensitivity to spectral scaling.

piezas.titulo: Sensory Processing Differences in Children With Idiopathic Toe Walking: A Scoping Review and Exploratory Meta-Analysis.
piezas.resumenOriginal: ImportanceThe cause of idiopathic toe walking (ITW) remains unclear, though impaired sensory processing has often been hypothesized to be linked to ITW.ObjectivesThe objective of this article is to review the literature on toe-walking to identify how sensory processing contributes to ITW.Data SourcesFour databases (CINAHL, Pubmed, PsychINFO, and SCOPUS) were searched for papers related to sensory processing and ITW published prior to July 2024. References of retrieved papers were reviewed for additional sources.Study Selection and Data CollectionThe PRISMA guidelines for scoping review were used to abstract the data following Joanna Briggs Institute methodology. Inclusion criteria were examined and papers included at least one sensory system related to ITW was studied. Papers were excluded if toe walking was due to diagnosed neurological, orthopedic, or genetic conditions.FindingsOur scoping review identified 13 published articles relevant to examining sensory processing in children with ITW. Studies explored differences in vibration perception, light touch, proprioception, vestibular, visual processing, sensorimotor functional assessments, and parental surveys of sensory processing. Six of the papers were included in a meta-analysis on vibration perception threshold that failed to reach significance ( p = .12). Despite heterogeneity across studies in participants, methods, and outcomes, a meta-analysis for atypical scores from parent-report sensory processing survey data yielded significant differences between children with ITW and typical controls ( p < .0068).Conclusions and RelevanceChildren with ITW demonstrate impairments across multiple domains of sensory processing and sensory-motor function suggesting an underlying relationship between ITW and sensory differences. Children with ITW, however, represent a diverse group of individuals with significant between-subjects variability in which senses are impaired, and which outcome measures best capture these differences.

piezas.titulo: Naturalistic Movie Viewing Reveals a Distributed Network Supporting Audiovisual Speech Processing
piezas.resumenOriginal: Traditional paradigms in cognitive neuroscience often fail to capture the richness of real-world experiences. To bridge this gap, researchers increasingly use naturalistic stimuli such as movies, which provide complex, multisensory input. Speech perception is a prime example of such complexity: it is inherently multisensory, involving the integration of auditory cues, lip movements, and facial expressions. Prior studies suggest that the left posterior superior temporal sulcus (pSTS) and superior temporal gyrus (STG) play a critical role in this integration. However, most studies of audiovisual speech have relied on simplified or artificial stimuli, limiting ecological validity. To address these gaps, we analyzed fMRI data from human participants watching two full-length films (500 Days of Summer, Citizenfour) to assess the consistency of multisensory speech processes across distinct genres and narratives. We manually annotated word onset times and modality (audiovisual vs. auditory-only). Across two movies and 38 participants we observed consistent speech-related activation in the pSTS and STG across speech types. Compared to auditory-only speech, audiovisual speech recruited a broad left-lateralized network including the angular gyrus, posterior temporal cortex, temporal pole, and inferior frontal gyrus, along with the right cerebellum. These findings were also consistently present in single-subject data. Importantly, most of the regions observed in our analyses have been implicated in multisensory function in the nonhuman primate literature despite receiving relatively little focus in human neuroimaging. Together our results demonstrate that speech processing during naturalistic viewing recruits a distributed network extending substantially beyond regions traditionally emphasized in audiovisual speech research.

piezas.titulo: Cortical responses to lipread and text-based audiovisual stimuli in adults with and without dyslexia
piezas.resumenOriginal: Phonetic recalibration enables listeners to adjust their perception of ambiguous speech sounds based on visual contextual information. In line with a specific difficulty in forming letter-speech sound associations, adults with dyslexia have been found to show no text-based, but intact lipread-based, recalibration. The underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear however. This fMRI study examined cortical responses during text-based and lipread-based phonetic recalibration in 34 adults (18 with dyslexia, 16 typical readers). Participants were exposed to ambiguous speech sounds /a?a/ paired with disambiguating visual information (“aba”/“ada” text or lipread videos), followed by auditory-only categorization trials. Contrary to previous findings, both groups showed robust text-based and lipread-based behavioral recalibration effects, with no significant group differences between typical and dyslexic readers. Neuroimaging data did yield group differences in the underlying cortical activation. Most notably, dyslexic readers demonstrated increased bilateral fusiform activation compared to typical readers during exposure to lipread videos and ambiguous speech sounds, with left fusiform activation specifically correlating with increased phonological processing difficulties. Additionally, typical readers exhibited higher right frontal activation during text-based audiovisual stimuli. These findings suggest that while adults with dyslexia did not differ significantly from typical readers in behavioral recalibration effects, they employed different neural processing strategies. Unexpectedly, this was particularly the case for lipread audiovisual stimuli. The relatively increased fusiform and superior temporal activation to lipread audiovisual stimuli in dyslexic readers possibly relates to subtle difficulties in phonological processing of ambiguous speech signals.

piezas.titulo: Bilateral cerebellar high-frequency rTMS for refractory epilepsy: a randomized, single-blind, sham-controlled study
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundFor patients with drug-resistant epilepsy who are not suitable for surgery, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is an important non-invasive neuromodulation therapy. The cerebellar cortex can inhibit cortical excitability via the cerebello-thalamo-cortical pathway. Here, we explore whether high-frequency (20 Hz) cerebellar repetitive TMS (rTMS) reduces seizure frequency and interictal epileptiform discharges (IEDs) in refractory epilepsy.MethodsEighty-seven patients with refractory epilepsy were included in the intention-to-treat (ITT) population (n = 87) and then randomized to active rTMS (n = 44) or sham stimulation (n = 43). One patient in treatment group had no post-baseline efficacy data; efficacy analyses were therefore performed in the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population (n = 86). The active group received two cycles of 20 Hz rTMS targeting the cerebellum. Seizure frequency and IEDs were assessed before and after treatment.ResultsPoisson generalized linear mixed models revealed a significant group×time interaction for seizure frequency [F(2,236) = 162.65, p < 0.001]. The active group had significantly lower seizure frequencies at months 1, 2, and 3 (all p < 0.001), with the largest difference at month 2. Percentage reductions of seizure frequency in the active group were 64.6%, 73.2%, and 13.3%, respectively, compared with 3.9%, 0.6%, and −8.4% in the control group (all P < 0.001). Responder rates (≥50% reduction) in the active group were 90.7%, 95.3%, and 0% vs. 0% in controls (p < 0.001 for months 1–2). Within-group analysis showed significant IED reduction after active rTMS (p < 0.001) but no change in controls. Moreover, a significant group × baseline interaction (p < 0.001) indicated greater suppression in patients with higher baseline IEDs. Exploratory subgroup analysis further confirmed this. All adverse events were mild, with no significant difference in the incidence between the two groups.ConclusionActive cerebellar rTMS was associated with reduced seizure frequency, improved responder rates, and suppressed IEDs in refractory epilepsy with no obvious discomfort. The optimal efficacy duration was approximately 2 months, with greater IED suppression in patients with higher baseline levels.

destilado.texto: No es solo una cuestión de resistencia a fármacos: la estimulación magnética cerebelosa también disminuye la frecuencia de convulsiones.
