piezas.titulo: Behind the scenes, two months later: How we ship Google Agent Skills like products
piezas.resumenOriginal:
In my previous post, I took you behind the scenes of Google Agent Skills , covering how the project started, how we maintain quality at scale, and how we handle governance. In this post, I'll share what we've built since then: the automated quality gates that every change must pass, the AI review agent that inspects skill quality, and the lessons that we learned along the way. You can adopt similar gates and review rules in your own skill repository. Since my last post, the Google Agent Skills repository has passed 21,000 GitHub stars, up from 15,000. It now hosts over 170 skills from teams across Google, and we distribute them across multiple AI platforms. Building agent skills for a single developer or a small project is straightforward. You write a SKILL.md file, define a few instructions, test it manually, and it works. At our scale, manual workflows stop being effective. Unvetted edits can introduce subtle bugs, and it becomes difficult to catch issues before they reach users. The core philosophy: Ship skills like products One key lesson from my previous post: a skill is a living product, not a one-off document. In practice, that means we ship every skill update like a product release. It's tempting to treat a skill as documentation. But documentation explains concepts to a human reader, while a skill steers an AI agent's reasoning loop, tool selection, and execution path. A misplaced phrase in a skill can cause an agent to invoke invalid command flags, enter an infinite loop, or waste tokens. That makes every instruction edit a behavioral change. You wouldn't ship a product update without testing it, and the same goes for a skill. This principle drives three core requirements: Strict semantic versioning : Every behavioral change requires an explicit version bump. Deterministic automated validation : Linters and validators check every proposed change before a human or AI reviewer sees it. Mandatory evaluation evidence : Every change includes an evaluation report. It compares the skill against its previous version, or—if the skill is new—against an agent without the skill. Automated conformance gates: The pull request pipeline In my previous post, I briefly listed the checks that every skill passes on check-in: linters, link checkers, and AI-assisted checklists. Here's what's inside them, plus two gates that I haven't covered before: semantic versioning and evaluation suite validation. When an author submits a change to our internal skills repository, an automated continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline triggers immediately. Before a skill is exported to GitHub, it must pass these six automated gates and receive human approval: Structural conformance : Directory layout, allowed files, and taxonomy. Skill linters : Frontmatter, folder naming, and Markdown rules. Semantic versioning : Version bump for every behavioral change. Evaluation suite : Valid eval suite and a fresh eval report. Link validation : Links are valid. AI review agent : Skill quality and design standards. Human approval : Final approval from a human reviewer (a subject matter expert) . Structural conformance and skill linters Our automated validation suite inspects every pull request for structural and syntactical correctness. Some of the rules include these requirements: Folder name and metadata name must match. SKILL.md and description length limits are enforced. All required fields in the frontmatter metadata are present. Only a curated list of files and directories is allowed within a skill directory. All Markdown files follow formatting rules. The main README.md file and the machine-readable index.json registry are up to date. Semantic versioning Every skill declares a semantic version in its SKILL.md frontmatter metadata: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '---
name: spanner-basics
metadata:
 version: "1.1.1"
 category: Databases
description: ...
---'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f2513c90310>)])]> First, our automated checks verify that the version is a quoted string. YAML parses unquoted values like 2.0 as numbers, which causes unexpected parsing errors in tools that expect a string. Second, the validator checks the version transition itself. New skills must start at 1.0.0 , and any change to an existing skill's instructions, scripts, or references requires a version bump or the pull request is blocked. Standard reset rules apply: bumping MAJOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 2.0.0 ) resets MINOR and PATCH to 0 , and bumping MINOR (for example, 1.4.2 to 1.5.0 ) resets PATCH to 0 . Why enforce strict versioning if the agent only reads the Markdown instructions? The version number is for the developer and their package tooling, not for the model at runtime. Skills don't auto-update in the background, which means there's no network check or latency overhead each time an agent invokes a skill. Instead, explicit versions let developers compare their locally installed skills against the upstream catalog and decide when to pull changes—for example, by running the npx skills update command. This versioning also supports workflows where teams want to lock a critical skill to a known-good version to guarantee reproducible agent behavior across their projects. Evaluation suite validation Our continuous evaluations (evals) compare agent performance with and without each skill. Those results are only as reliable as the evaluation suites behind them. If a suite contains broken file references or compound expectations, test results become noisy and untrustworthy. Our validator parses each evaluation suite and the pull request description. Then it checks several strict invariants: Resolution of file-based prompts : When a test prompt references a file (such as @file:test_prompt.txt ), the validator confirms that the target file exists and that it isn't empty. Atomic expectations : Each expectation must check exactly one criterion. The validator blocks compound expectations until authors split them. Lesson 2 later in this post shows why. Duplicate detection : The validator flags duplicate test prompts and conflicting expectations within the same evaluation suite. Mandatory evaluation report : Every pull request that modifies a skill must link to an evaluation report in its description. Eval staleness check : Authors usually iterate on a pull request as reviewers leave feedback. The validator confirms that the linked report ran against the latest commit. Link validation Over 170 skills link to documentation for fast-evolving Google products, and those pages can move long after a skill passes review. Rather than waiting for users to report broken links, we validate links at two stages. Before merge, pull request checks verify all relative links, such as files in references/ . Then, every Monday, a GitHub Actions workflow runs lychee across all external links in the public repository and it reports any broken links to skill owners for remediation. AI review agent Linters and schema validators catch syntactic errors, but they can't evaluate overall quality. They can't tell you if an instruction is confusing, if a reference guide is too verbose, or if a task should have been a bash script instead of a large language model (LLM) instruction. To solve this, we integrated an AI review agent into our review pipeline. When a change affects a skill, the AI reviewer inspects it using a dedicated review skill. Yes, we use a skill to review skills. Here are the core rules the AI reviewer evaluates. You can adopt these rules in your own skill development workflows. 1. Skill suitability and the deterministic trap The first question our AI reviewer asks is simple: Does this task belong in an instruction? We often see authors fall into the deterministic trap . They write rigid, numbered sequences of command-line interface (CLI) commands directly into Markdown text. LLMs are probabilistic engines. If an operation requires a strict sequence of commands where a variation can cause an error, embedding those commands in the instruction text invites hallucinations. Our AI reviewer enforces a clear boundary between deterministic and probabilistic logic. Rigid CLI sequences, JSON parsers, and deployment steps must live in executable scripts under scripts/ . Markdown instructions are reserved for tasks that require judgment, such as choosing an architecture, diagnosing error logs, or synthesizing code. This rule complements the Model Context Protocol (MCP) guidance that I shared last time: prefer remote MCP tools whenever possible. When you must fall back to CLI or API calls, wrap them in a script instead of spelling them out in the instructions. 2. The L1/L2/L3 modular architecture Context windows are valuable. Loading a 2,000-line skill into an agent consumes context and degrades reasoning. Our AI reviewer enforces a three-tier information hierarchy that follows the progressive disclosure model of Agent Skills: Level 1 (Metadata) : The YAML frontmatter ( name , description ). The agent uses this concise summary for discovery and routing. Level 2 (Core instructions) : The main SKILL.md file. The body must stay compact (under 500 lines). It provides workflow overviews, decision trees, and guardrails. Level 3 (Reference docs) : Detailed API references, schemas, and other reference tables live in a references/ directory. Our AI reviewer enforces two distinct rules for Level 3: flat directory structure and single-hop indirection . Keeping references/ flat (no subdirectories) is a repository convention that discourages sprawling documentation trees and makes file discovery simpler. More importantly for runtime performance, the reviewer blocks chained references , where SKILL.md links to a reference file that links to yet another file. Each hop requires an extra tool call, adding latency and cost, and our evaluations showed that agents frequently stop before following a second level of chained references. 3. Non-interactive script design When skills bundle helper scripts in scripts/ , we expect agents to execute them directly in terminal sandboxes. Our AI reviewer flags any script that blocks on interactive prompts. Every script must accept inputs through command-line flags or environment variables, provide --help documentation, and include a --dry-run or confirmation flag for destructive operations. Scripts also need to separate output cleanly, writing structured data (usually JSON) to standard output and writing actionable error messages to standard error. Example AI review checklist snippet The review skill also checks frontmatter for spec compliance and discovery, and it turns the L1/L2/L3 architecture into concrete structure rules. Here's an excerpt from those criteria: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '### Front Matter & Discovery

- **Spec Compliance**: YAML front matter MUST strictly follow the Agent Skills
 Reference Specification (https://agentskills.io/specification). Use `>-`
 (folded strip-chomping) format for multi-line descriptions.
- **Description Quality**: The `description` field must follow the
 [Description Guide](references/description_guide.md).

### Content Structure & Authoring Quality

- **L1/L2/L3 Architecture**: Enforce modular structure. The main `SKILL.md`
 body must stay under 500 lines. Move deep domain reference material to
 `references/` (see [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
- **Flat References Directory**: `references/` must be a flat directory (one
 level deep, no nested subdirectories). References > 100 lines must include a
 Table of Contents with line hints (see
 [Skill Structure](references/skill_structure.md)).
- **Avoid Deeply-Nested References**: Avoid deeply-nested references (e.g.,
 `SKILL.md` -> `references/guides.md` -> `assets/output.tmpl`). Keep
 reference structures shallow (one level of indirection from `SKILL.md`)
 because agents might not load such link targets fully.'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f25182ad7d0>)])]> Human approval After it passes all automated checks, every pull request must receive approval from a human reviewer. The reviewer is typically the skill's subject matter expert and, for new skills, a member of the Central Skills team. Lessons learned from repository history Six months of commit history and pull request discussions reveal several practical takeaways. 1. Scope CI checks carefully Early in the project, we configured automated pull request checks with broad directory patterns. One check required an approved bug tracking ticket on every change. Because the pattern matched too broadly, engineers making a one-line typo fix were blocked for missing a tracking ticket. Meanwhile, newly added skills in deeper subdirectories went uninspected. Takeaway : Match automated check rules to specific file operations, such as added versus modified files, and verify exact path depths. Treat minor edits to existing skills differently from new skills. 2. Atomic expectations When we started writing evaluation suites, we saw authors write compound expectations like this: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Bad: Compound expectation
- "The agent must create a Cloud Storage bucket in us-central1, enable
 uniform bucket-level access, and apply lifecycle rules."'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f25182ac7d0>)])]> If the agent configured the region and lifecycle rules but missed the uniform access flag, the LLM-as-a-judge scorer returned inconsistent ratings. Migrating to atomic expectations resolved the inconsistent ratings: code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', '# Good: Atomic expectations
- "The agent specifies us-central1 for the bucket location."
- "The agent enables uniform bucket-level access on the created bucket."
- "The agent defines a lifecycle configuration rule deleting objects
 older than 30 days."'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f25182ae090>)])]> Takeaway : Check exactly one criterion per expectation. Atomic expectations make evaluation results clear, reliable, and debuggable. 3. Documentation drift happens fast In a multi-contributor repository, documentation tables drift within days if maintained manually. Takeaway : If you publish an index or catalog, never rely on contributors to update it manually. Instead, write a generator script and enforce it with a CI unit test. That's the origin of the README.md and index.json checks in our linters. Our index.json even opens with a warning: "This file is generated. Do not edit it by hand." 4. Gate expensive LLM checks behind fast deterministic ones Running full evaluation suites and an AI review agent on every change can get expensive fast, both in token usage and CI runtime—especially when authors push frequent small commits during review. In our pipeline, fast deterministic checks run first. Structural conformance, skill linters, and semantic versioning act as blocking gates: if any of them fail, the pipeline stops immediately and it won't trigger the AI reviewer or evaluation checks until those issues are fixed. Takeaway : Stage your pipeline so cheap, deterministic checks block broken changes before LLM-powered gates run. When you build a similar system, consider adding further cost guardrails, such as manual triggers for heavy checks (for example, a /run-evals pull request comment) or only triggering automatic re-runs when the diff exceeds a specific threshold. Conclusion Building a scalable Agent Skills repository requires more than good prompt engineering. It requires solid developer infrastructure: Ship skills like products: version, validate, and evaluate every change. Enforce semantic versioning and atomic expectations with automated CI gates. Use an AI reviewer to catch design anti-patterns, such as the deterministic trap. Check links before merge and on a schedule. piezas.titulo: Changes in Functional and Health-Related Outcomes After a Disability-Delay Program Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background: Frailty, sarcopenia, and cognitive decline are associated with reduced functional independence and participation among older adults. Occupational therapy uses multidomain and participation-focused approaches to support functional independence and healthy aging; however, evidence regarding functional and health-related changes among community-dwelling older adults participating in structured multidomain programs remains limited. This study aimed to describe pre-post changes in functional and health-related outcomes and to explore associations among concurrent changes in these measures. Methods: This uncontrolled retrospective pre-post program evaluation analyzed routinely collected data from 60 community-dwelling older adults who participated in a 12-week occupational therapist-led multidomain community program at five community sites. The program was delivered once weekly for 2 h and incorporated cognitive, physical, and daily activity-related components. Functional ability, frailty, sarcopenia risk, grip strength, cognitive function, and health-related quality of life were assessed at baseline and program completion. Pre-post differences were examined using paired-samples t -tests, and separate age-adjusted linear regression models were used to examine associations between individual clinical change variables and concurrent changes in functional outcomes. Results: Pre-post differences were observed in activities of daily living, frailty, sarcopenia risk, grip strength, cognitive function, and health-related quality of life. In separate exploratory age-adjusted regression models, changes in frailty (SOF), sarcopenia risk (SARC-F), and cognitive function (SPMSQ) were associated with concurrent changes in selected functional outcomes. These associations were considered exploratory and should not be interpreted as evidence of independent prediction or causality. Conclusions: Pre-post changes in multiple functional and health-related outcomes were observed among community-dwelling older adults participating in the 12-week occupational therapist-led multidomain program. Given the uncontrolled retrospective pre-post design, the observed changes cannot be attributed to the program, and the associations among concurrent changes should not be interpreted as causal. These findings may inform occupational therapy practice and the development of community-based multidomain programs aimed at supporting functional independence and participation in daily life. Further prospective controlled studies are needed to confirm these findings and determine whether such programs produce clinically meaningful changes in functional and health-related outcomes.

piezas.titulo: Peer Mentoring Benefits in Rehabilitation for Individuals With Spinal Cord Injury: A Systematic Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Importance The lived experiences of peer mentors with spinal cord injury (SCI) provide distinct value in the rehabilitation process and contribute to improved outcomes. When combined with traditional therapy, peer mentorship programs can enhance life satisfaction among individuals living with SCI. Objective To explore the impact that peer-led mentorship programs and interventions have on the rehabilitation outcomes for individuals with a spinal cord injury (SCI). Data sources PubMed, MEDLINE, PsycINFO, CINAHL, ERIC, Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, MedNar, and OpenGrey were searched between 2014 and 2024. The Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool was adapted and used to assess risk of bias in the included studies. Study selection and data collection Inclusion criteria included individuals with SCI who participated in peer mentorship and reported outcomes on quality of life, well-being, independence, or activities of daily living (ADLs) or instrumental ADLs. Exclusion criteria included interventions conducted via telehealth or reported outcomes of social participation. Findings Five articles were analyzed for synthesis, which included individuals 18 yr and older with an SCI. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Findings may have limited generalizability across different settings and populations because of the small number of available studies and variability in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures. None of the articles reviewed included occupational therapists. Conclusions and relevance This review highlighted the benefits of peer mentorship in enhanced life satisfaction. Findings support peer mentorship as an important component of rehabilitation. Future research should examine the benefits of incorporating peer-led intervention programs across the continuum of care, including occupational therapy, in enhancing best practices in SCI rehabilitation. Plain-Language Summary: Peer mentorship programs can help people with spinal cord injuries adjust to daily life by providing guidance, support, and encouragement that professionals without lived experience may not offer. This review found that peer mentoring can improve psychological well-being and health management and reduce unplanned hospital visits. Evidence is limited because of the small number of studies and variations in study design; however, the results suggest that meaningful benefits may be present. Further research is needed to determine the most effective way to implement peer mentorship across rehabilitation settings.

piezas.titulo: Fragments: October 28
piezas.resumenOriginal: Andrej Karpathy sees a widening gap in how people see LLM capabilities. The general public has mostly not interacted with these systems. When they have, it looks like a derpy chatbot. The majority of professionals still see only a modest uplift. And a small sliver of professionals are experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical. And it is all happening at the same time. Many of my colleagues are living in a world where LLM capabilities are stunning, but it’s easy to forget that’s not what most people experience. One thing I do is use free-tier LLM chatbots, and I’m still finding that while most of the time they are useful, their unreliability undermines much of that usefulness. Yes, you can argue that I’m not using frontier tools or a forceful enough harness, but that’s true of most regular folks too. To understand their perception, it’s handy to experience it. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ That observation particularly resonates with me today, as I’ve just spent the weekend at Foocamp, an open space event run by O’Reilly. It was full of those who are experiencing that vertigo of LLM capabilities, so it felt very much like being in a bubble of those on the bleeding edge. While it’s worth remembering that that’s not a typical view of what’s happening, it’s good to see what those explorers are experiencing. (As I talk about this, I’m applying the Chatham House rule , if anyone wants attribution, let me know.) A couple of folks talked about doing immersion courses to help teach developers how to do agentic engineering . The idea is to get people out of their usual work environment, and spend one or two weeks with experienced coaches, learning how to use these tools well. Such things remind me very much of the Extreme Programming immersion classes I was involved with at the turn of the century. As with that, the experience of building something is important to understand such a new style of work. Unsurprisingly the coaches observed that the biggest impact wasn’t technical, but emotional. New tools are just new tools, but these tools change basic assumptions of what it means to be a software developer, which for many people challenges their identity. One coach said how his main job was to take such people out for a walk to a coffee shop, so they could process what’s happening. (This reminds me of a participant of the Extreme Programming immersion who was so horrified by the use of a non-locking version-control system (CVS) that he walked out of the class on the first day.) ❄ ❄ I’m wary of talking about themes to an event where I attend less than one-tenth of the sessions, but a topic I kept coming across was how large enterprises were embracing this technology - or rather not. One participant used a lovely metaphor: corporations have acquired a Swiss-army knife, but are only using the toothpick. I see plenty of decent reasons for this: it’s one thing for a startup or individual to use a hot technology, but there’s a big difference between a website going down and your factories grinding to a halt. Big organizations involve workflows involving lots of people that have built up over many years - they don’t change easily. Security concerns abound, the lethal trifecta still lurks. In particular good use of AI in enterprises relies on good data, and many such organizations don’t have their data in a decent shape. The path to getting agent-ready data isn’t trivial and it’s hard to see how we can get the knife and saw out until enterprises are much further down that path. One thing that struck me is that there was little conversation about this at Foocamp - a sign of its visibility among the people there. ❄ ❄ I very much enjoyed Foocamp, but events like this are always a mix of excitement and dread. I knew very few of the people there, so it was a great opportunity to get out of my own social bubble. But I also find it nearly impossible to walk up to people I don’t know (or know slightly) and impose my company on them. The great thing about unconferences is that the nature of the sessions make it plausible for someone like me to engage in conversation during them, and begin some tentative links. Also I thank the many folks there who were friendly to me as I casually walked around trying to hide how much I was panicking. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Laurie Voss says today is 1997 On Saturday, Apollo’s chief economist Torsten Slok published No Signs of AI Payoff Outside the Tech Sector. It’s short and it’s blunt: outside of 7 major tech companies, there is no data yet to support a productivity gain that justifies all the money pouring into tech. My position is that he’s half right: are valuations too high? Absolutely. We’re in a bubble, and it’s absolutely going to pop. But does that mean investing in AI is a waste of money? Absolutely not, and using this early data to try and decide that question would be like trying to decide in 1997 whether the Internet was going to pay off. The data just isn’t there yet, because these things take time. I’m not as sure as he is that we can peg today to 1997 rather than 1999, but I agree that this boom bears a lot of resemblance to the dotcom boom (although I think this one is bigger). While many dotcom companies crashed (I always think of pets.com and webvan) he’s right to point out that anyone who invested in Amazon in 1997 did very well. Where might those good investments be this time? if you can build something that proves you got the answer, AI can get the answer much faster than you can, and there are real productivity gains to be had doing that generally. As we think about this, remember that investment isn’t just buying shares, but also where we choose to invest that precious resource of our time and energy. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Adam Tornhill asks Were All Those Years of Coding Wasted? For me, agentic coding is enjoyable because it lets me take on larger parts of a problem than I would have been able to master manually. Infrastructure updates are no longer a blocker. And I don’t need to spend time learning about a build system I never cared about. My personal goal is to get better at working with higher-level abstractions, and accept that writing code is likely to be a dying skill. My bet on the future is that our problem solving skills, logical mindset, and understanding of systems will be at least as rewarding. In the end, we only need to challenge our identity if we mistake programming for writing code. AI finally allows us to separate the two. And that’s where all those years of experience transfer the best: knowing not only what to build but how to build it well. ❄ ❄ Tim Bray looks at this from another direction For me (and I’m not alone), the biggest issue isn’t what GenAI can and can’t do, it’s the ethical and economic discomforts. This technology is being peddled by terrible people who are rich and whose goal is to get richer. It’s bought and deployed by terrible people who want to slash their payrolls by throwing thought workers onto the street. It facilitates the oncoming climate catastrophe and devalues human creative effort. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ Annie Vella observes that the change we’re seeing in software development follows a way of thinking about automation that goes back to the 1960’s as the distinction between direct and supervisory control . The main difference between direct and supervisory control is that in the latter, there’s a computer that closes the loop instead of a human operator. Before AI, writing software was much more like direct control - we closed the loop ourselves. We interpreted requirements, made changes to the code, received feedback and acted on it, over and over. Now, coding agents can increasingly close that loop themselves - writing code, running tests and fixing their own mistakes - while we move towards supervisory control: telling the agent what we want, keeping an eye on how it’s going and taking over when we need to. She outlines various ideas that this intellectual thread developed. The five-level model developed by Endsley and Kiris seems apposite: Level Human System In AI-assisted software development 1. None Decide, act - No AI assistance 2. Decision support Decide, act Suggest The early days of AI coding assistants’ autocomplete 3. Consensual AI Concur Decide, act AI coding agents where you must approve the actions they take 4. Monitored AI Veto Decide, act Auto-mode, with the ability to veto the coding agent’s actions 5. Full automation - Decide, act Full auto-mode, such as might be used in a dark software factory Vella cautions that this comes with an important caveat: There is one notable difference between the automation described by this prior research and the type of automation that AI agents give us. Both sets of levels assume that the computer’s account of what it did is accurate and honest. As we all know by now, what an AI agent says it did and what it actually did may not be the same thing. Still, it’s automation, and it still requires supervision - arguably more, since we can’t simply take its word for it. Vella’s conclusion from all this is that: “our next step must be to start redesigning the job and the system, in tandem”. I agree with this, and the Foocampers’ immersion courses I mentioned earlier are part of that exercise. The tricky thing is that we don’t yet know what this new job design looks like, but I think Vella is on the right path when she says: What if we stopped thinking of the SDLC as a process we follow, and instead started thinking of it as a control system we build and supervise? ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ A while ago I mentioned how much I enjoyed Eric Evans’s keynote at DDD Europe. Now the video is available so those who weren’t in Antwerp can watch it. He opens by looking at our future, saying that rather than fruitlessly trying to predict it, we should instead explore it with “curiosity, fun, and wonder”. He’s been doing this, digging deeper into the theory and fundamentals that underpin AI. He goes into detail on his side project: the Domain Language Surveyor. The idea is to be able to examine different repositories, and analyze the vocabulary used inside those repositories to see if they are related bounded contexts . To do this he built a pipeline of tools, illustrating how a useful system blends both computational and inferential components. He then used this pipeline to analyze the vocabulary of some open-source healthcare codebases, to see how their bounded contexts related. ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ ❄ A topic that regularly comes up when I talk to companies outside the Foocamp world, is the cost of tokens, and the concern about how that cost is going to increase in the future. We’ve been worrying about that at Thoughtworks, and my colleague Andy Nolan describes our token sourcing strategy , which we forecast will reduce our token costs in 2028 from $16-40M down to $6.8-1M. The strategy rents frontier models for the work that needs frontier-level reasoning. It runs open-weight models, on capacity we choose, for the work that carries our IP or runs at a volume where owning the capacity costs less. The strategy involves looking at each LLM workload, and classifying it on two axes: domain differentiation and security & sovereignty. We then place each workload on a nine cell grid. The nine cells run from the cheapest capable API, swapped as prices change, to a fine-tuned open model on our own infrastructure, with full control and full upkeep. For a given workload, the highest score on a given axis determines the right position in the grid. There is no single right place for all workloads. Each organization ends up with its own distribution and mix of workloads across the grid.

piezas.titulo: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum
piezas.resumenOriginal: Two Nonprofits Join Forces to Support Adolescents on Autism Spectrum STAR Admin Thu, 06/15/2017 - 14:07 STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder (SPD) and T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades) are two Colorado nonprofits who have partnered to create a series of respite camps serving adolescents who have autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Developmental Pathways has awarded the organizations a $25,000 grant to fund three F.U.S.E. (Fostering Unlimited Success and Empowerment) camps through 2018. STAR Institute offers premier treatment for SPD and brings expertise in social skills while T.AC.T. teaches trade and life skills to individuals with ASD and SPD with an emphasis on fostering independence and personal growth. “This is a very rare and exciting way to see two nonprofits interact. Our partnership to create F.U.S.E. allows both of our organizations to combine expertise in a way that best serves these adolescents to find new interests and gain the soft skills to successfully participate in peer groups and future workplaces”, says Dick Layton, Director of STAR Institute for SPD. The respite camps will be week-long day camps that host six students per camp ages 12-15 who have autism spectrum disorder. The camps will teach pre-vocational and vocational skills in a supportive, social, and inclusionary environment. Each camp has a different project for participants including: building a non-motorized go-cart with a partner, building an instrument to play in a band, and crafting board games. “The intended focus of F.U.S.E. is not just about offering a respite program for families. By generating new experiences for these adolescents, we hope to foster new skills, new interests, develop social skills, and give them a sense of empowerment to participate in what hopefully becomes a new hobby or future career interest”, says Danny Combs co-founder and president of T.A.C.T. SPD is a neurological disorder that disrupts the way an individual processes and responds to sensations. The disorder can affect people in only one sense–for example, just touch or just sight or just movement–or in multiple senses. One person with SPD may over-respond to touch sensation and find clothing, physical contact, other tactile sensory input to be unbearable and/or they may respond to visual or auditory or another sensory input. Another person might under-respond and show little or no reaction to stimulation, even pain or extreme hot and cold or just may be slow to respond to sensation. SPD and ASD have a high co-morbidity rate, but are also found to be standalone disorders. ASD refers to conditions categorized by challenges with social skills, repetitive behaviors, speech and nonverbal communication, as well as by unique strengths and differences that can occur on a range from mild to severe. Individuals with ASD and SPD frequently struggle with interpersonal skills over their lifetime and are often underestimated, which can lead to specific difficulty in career and relationships. F.U.S.E. aims to give individuals the ability to ignite new interests and feel empowered in group collaboration, which can lead to greater success in career and relationships. About STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder: The STAR Institute for Sensory Processing Disorder, a Colorado 501(c)(3), is the world leader in treatment, research, and education for Sensory Processing Disorder, a neurological condition that disrupts the daily lives of more than 4 million Americans. The STAR Institute is the premier treatment center for children, adults and families living with Sensory Processing Disorder, feeding disorders, and other sensory conditions associated with ADHD, autism, and other developmental disorders. Dr. Lucy Jane Miller, founder of STAR Institute, is widely recognized as the leader in Sensory Processing Disorder research worldwide. For more information about the Greenwood Village, Colorado clinic, visit http://www.spdSTAR.org or call 303-221-7827. About T.A.C.T. (Teaching the Autism Community Trades): T.A.C.T is a 501(c)(3) that provides trade and technical skills to children, young adults and families living with Autism Spectrum Disorder. Early vocational training helps young adults before they leave high school and sets them up for long term success. Our programs are designed to empower individuals and develop interests and skills for life. To learn more visit: https://tactkids.org or call 720-460-0897. About Developmental Pathways: Developmental Pathways is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit agency serving individuals with developmental disabilities/delays and their families. We are also one of Colorado’s Community Centered Boards (CCB) connecting people to federal, state, county, and private funding in Arapahoe County, Douglas County, and the City of Aurora. We passionately believe inclusion is for everyone and offer services through Home and Community Based Medicaid Waiver programs, locally funded programs, and partnerships with other community organizations. To learn more visit: http://www.dpcolo.org by STAR Institute for SPD Sensory Processing Disorder

piezas.titulo: Master AI Chip Principles With New IEEE Design Program
piezas.resumenOriginal: Today’s engineers face an unprecedented acceleration in AI hardware complexity, as explained in the recent research article “ Revisiting Edge AI: Opportunities and Challenges .” The article examines the rapid growth of edge AI and the challenges it creates, including resource constraints, model architecture limitations, and network demands across edge-AI deployments. The acceleration is driven by a fundamental shift in how modern AI models are built and scaled. As the models have become much larger and more complex, they are computationally more demanding because they contain more parameters and require more calculations. To meet the demands of scaling deep neural networks, the industry is increasingly developing AI chips that are designed for specific tasks. One major reason is that moving data between memory and the processor has become a major limitation on AI performance. The movement to confront the hardware bottleneck—the AI memory wall —has altered the trajectory of semiconductor innovation, shifting architectural priorities toward domain-specific accelerator platforms. No longer can engineers evaluate systems statically; they must master joint hardware design and network-algorithm co-optimization to navigate the critical trade‑offs between throughput, latency, and operational efficiency. The challenges are addressed in the new AI Processor Architecture, Design Principles, and Performance program , developed by IEEE Educational Activities with support from the IEEE Computer Society . Topics covered The five-course program provides a structured exploration of AI processor technologies, from fundamental design principles to advanced architectures and real-world deployment. The topics are: Fundamental principles of design and functionality. Practical insights into advanced architectures. Understanding neural processing units for industry deployment. Emerging trends and evolving architectures. Designing for edge, cloud, quantum, and the Internet of Things (IoT). The program addresses the needs of professionals across the AI hardware ecosystem, including hardware architects, chip designers, embedded systems developers, data‑center hardware engineers, and innovators exploring next‑generation processor ecosystems. It is also valuable for those transitioning into AI chip design or seeking to understand the architectural forces shaping modern machine learning acceleration. For many, it provides the bridge between theoretical knowledge and the collaborative, cross‑disciplinary reasoning required in engineering environments. The program is designed to explore how modern AI processors are conceived, structured, and optimized. The architectural layers that define contemporary AI hardware will be covered, including compute units, memory hierarchies, dataflows, and the performance characteristics that emerge from design decisions. The curriculum bridges theory and application, enabling participants to interpret architectural foundations, analyze trade‑offs, and understand how hardware structures shape computational efficiency across diverse environments. By the end of the courses, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. AI-generated avatars explain concepts The program also uses a dialogue‑driven learning approach. Learners view conversations between AI-generated avatars that engage in scenario‑based dialogues. The avatars represent engineers tackling the same problems from various perspectives based on their different roles. The simulated storytelling and dialogues make advanced engineering concepts approachable without sacrificing depth or interactivity, because the user is occasionally challenged to decide the correct answer that leads to the best course of action. A hardware engineer might push back against a systems engineer’s demands, for example, revealing the friction between physical constraints and algorithmic ambition. A computational validation specialist might interrogate a chip performance engineer’s optimism, exposing the gap between theoretical throughput and real‑world behavior. A heterogeneous systems architect could debate a multiprocessor coordination specialist about synchronization overheads, while a standards development engineer discusses regulatory implications with a technology strategy and compliance architect. In the final course, an IoT systems architect and an embedded AI optimization engineer dissect the realities of deploying AI in constrained environments. By the end of the course, learners will be able to evaluate processor behavior with the analytical precision expected of professionals working at the frontier of AI hardware design. The avatar-driven learning environment creates a psychologically safer environment for learners, who might feel intimidated by traditional expert‑led videos. piezas.titulo: Designing Memory Architecture for Stateful AI Agents: Short-Term Context and Long-Term Persistence
piezas.resumenOriginal: A language model holds nothing between calls. Each request arrives with no memory of the previous one, and the model responds from the prompt in front of it and nothing more. For a one-shot question, that is fine. For an agent a person returns to across days, threads, and separate tasks, it becomes the defining design constraint. The behavior users expect from an agent, recalling what they said last week, resuming a task that stalled, applying their stated preferences without being asked again, is precisely the behavior a stateless model cannot produce on its own. A large language model (LLM) does not forget your context because it chose to. It never had it. The reflex fix is to paste the history back in. Keep a buffer of prior turns and prepend it to every prompt, so the agent looks like it remembers. That illusion survives a short demo and breaks in production. Building stateful AI agents that hold continuity across sessions takes a memory architecture, not a bigger buffer.

piezas.titulo: Turning behavior links cognitive and motor function to safe mobility post-stroke: a cross-sectional mediation analysis
piezas.resumenOriginal: IntroductionTurning behavior is the fundamental component of safe mobility. Despite rehabilitation, nearly three-fourths of falls after stroke occur during turning maneuvers. Consequently, individuals with stroke experience persistent mobility limitations, highlighting turning as a clinically important yet comparatively under-assessed determinant of safe mobility. Because turning engages both cognitive and motor systems, it may serve as a key link between these functions and safe mobility. The current study examined whether turning is linked to safe mobility and mediates the associations between cognitive function, motor function, and safe mobility after stroke.MethodsOne hundred and five stroke survivors participated in this study. Turning behavior was characterized by turn duration, turn angle, and peak turning velocity measured during dual-task walking. Safe mobility was assessed using Timed Up-and-Go (TUG) duration, Berg Balance Scale (BBS), gait speed, and gait variability score. We used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to compute latent scores for safe mobility. Cognitive function was assessed using an extensive neuropsychological battery. Motor function was evaluated using dorsiflexion and plantarflexion strength and motor accuracy on a goal-directed ankle task. We computed the composite score for turning behavior, cognitive, and motor functions. We conducted linear regression to examine the association between turning behavior and safe mobility, and mediation analyses to test whether turning behavior mediates the relationships of cognitive and motor function with safe mobility.ResultPoorer turning behavior was associated with compromised safe mobility (R2 = 0.66). Mediation analysis revealed that turning mediated the relationship between cognitive function and safe mobility (indirect effect; b = 0.29, SE = 0.11, CI: 0.08 to 0.54). Similarly, turning mediated the relationship between motor function and safe mobility (indirect effect; b = 0.40, SE = 0.10, CI: 0.22 to 0.63).ConclusionTurning behavior is a significant predictor of safe mobility post-stroke. Moreover, turning is a key pathway through which cognitive and motor impairments influence safe mobility after stroke. These findings suggest that incorporating turning-specific training may be an important consideration in gait rehabilitation post-stroke.

piezas.titulo: Imaging findings and clinical outcomes in neonates with isolated subependymal echogenicity on cranial ultrasound: a retrospective cohort study
piezas.resumenOriginal: ObjectiveTo describe clinical and imaging findings in neonates with isolated subependymal echogenicity on cranial ultrasound and examine associations with recorded mortality and cerebral palsy.MethodsThis retrospective single-center cohort included 317 neonates admitted between January 2015 and December 2018 with an initial ultrasound finding suspicious for isolated subependymal hemorrhage. Clinical records, available MRI findings, and follow-up information were reviewed. Cerebral palsy was ascertained from rehabilitation or neurology diagnostic records, supplemented by telephone follow-up in January 2026, independently of developmental test scores. The primary adjusted analysis compared death with all survivors using an exploratory six-item comorbidity count and clinical covariates; hospitalization duration was excluded, and laterality was coded as unilateral or bilateral.ResultsThere were 52 deaths (16.4%), 9 survivors with recorded cerebral palsy (2.8%), and 256 survivors without recorded cerebral palsy (80.8%). MRI findings were compatible with hemorrhage in 61 of 90 examined infants (67.8%). In the complete-case mortality model (n = 316), each additional comorbidity was associated with greater odds of death (adjusted OR, 2.462; 95% CI, 1.787–3.391; p < 0.001). The other included covariates were not statistically significant. White matter abnormalities were recorded in nine infants, including eight of the nine infants with cerebral palsy and one without recorded cerebral palsy.ConclusionSystemic comorbidity burden was associated with mortality within this ultrasound-defined cohort. White matter abnormalities accompanied most recorded cerebral palsy cases, but this observation remains descriptive. Specialist diagnostic records and later telephone follow-up characterize persistent clinical diagnoses; they do not establish the independent effect of subependymal echogenicity or normal development across all domains in survivors without cerebral palsy.

piezas.titulo: Cholinergic and adrenergic modulation sculpts parallel inhibition of SST-INs in visual cortex
piezas.resumenOriginal: GABAergic interneurons are fundamental to the normal function of neuronal circuits in the neocortex. A growing literature has highlighted the role of somatostatin-expressing interneurons (SST-INs) in regulating cortical activity, and inhibition of SST-INs by other interneurons has emerged as a circuit motif leading to disinhibition of pyramidal neurons. However, the diversity and regulation of GABAergic inputs to SST-INs are only partially understood. Here, we combined widefield and 2-photon optogenetic stimulation of parvalbumin (PV)- and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)-expressing interneurons with recordings from fluorescently identified SST-INs in layer 2/3 of primary visual cortex (V1). Our results show that both PV- and VIP-INs form inhibitory inputs onto SST-INs but with varying functional properties. PV-INs evoke strong, fast inhibition onto perisomatic regions of their target cells, while VIP-INs evoke slower inhibition onto target cell dendrites that is partially mediated by alpha subunit-containing GABA receptors. Cholinergic modulation through muscarinic receptors strongly suppresses PV-IN output while adrenergic modulation through beta receptors enhances VIP-IN output. Computational modeling suggests that these parallel inhibitory pathways can differentially regulate circuit gain and network stability across different inputs and arousal conditions. Thus, the diversity of disinhibitory GABAergic circuits in the neocortex provides a mechanism for state-dependent flexibility in circuit function.

piezas.titulo: Home Assessment Instruments in Occupational Therapy: A Scoping Review.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Background/objective The home environment should foster the independence, participation, and safety of its inhabitants. However, the presence of environmental barriers, especially for individuals with disabilities, can negatively impact their functioning, reducing well-being and quality of life at home. Occupational therapy plays a crucial role in this context, offering holistic evaluation processes and strategies for effective home modifications to improve occupational performance. To our knowledge, no comprehensive mapping of these tools exists. Therefore, this study conducts a scoping review to map and critically describe the home assessment instruments currently used within the field of occupational therapy. Methods A scoping review following a systematized approach was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA-ScR recommendations for scoping reviews, involving an online bibliographic search complemented by the consultation of grey literature. A two-phase screening process was performed to systematically identify the instruments referenced. Results Ninety-three articles were included, identifying twenty-nine home assessment tools applied in occupational therapy. These instruments presented notable differences in their format, target population, aspects assessed, and the degree of user participation during the evaluation process, among other characteristics. Conclusion This scoping review mapped 29 home assessment tools, revealing a strong focus on environmental factors but a critical gap in assessing personal factors, occupations, and social roles. While most instruments demonstrate acceptable reliability and validity, there is an urgent need for more robust psychometric studies, tools validated as clinical outcome measures, and the cultural adaptation of holistic, person-centered assessments to effectively guide home modifications. piezas.titulo: How Top-Down Are We? Reconsidering the Gap Between Occupational Therapy's Identity and Practice.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Occupational therapy has spent more than a century defining occupation as its professional core. Yet studies across countries and settings show a recurring gap. Therapists value occupation-centered practice while often relying on impairment-focused assessment and intervention. This article argues that the profession may face a translation problem more than an identity problem. Biomedical service structures, standardized measurement, workplace culture, and professional socialization can pull reasoning toward body functions. Bottom-up methods are not inherently incompatible with occupational therapy; the problem arises when change in a component is treated as sufficient evidence of occupational success. Drawing on occupational therapy research, the International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, rehabilitation science, and disability rights, we argue that occupation and participation should remain the outcomes that organize assessment, intervention, and evaluation. Practical changes are proposed for clinical reasoning, outcome measurement, education, supervision, and service design.

piezas.titulo: Multi-region two-photon calcium imaging in freely moving animals
piezas.resumenOriginal: Complex behaviors emerge from the coordinated activity of neural circuits distributed across widely separated brain regions. Existing optical approaches for monitoring neural activity lack the combined capability to record from anatomically distributed regions with high spatiotemporal resolution in freely moving animals. Here we introduce MINI2P-II, a 1.1-g 2P miniscope that achieves large-scale calcium imaging with high spatial resolution, deep imaging depth and dual-color imaging capability. Together with a dual-scope imaging system and a novel implantable periscope lens assembly, MINI2P-II enables simultaneous 2P imaging in widely separated or anatomically adjacent brain regions. In mice, we demonstrate inter-hemisphere coordination in bilateral motor cortex during climbing, egocentric boundary coding in simultaneous retrosplenial and posterior parietal cortex recordings, and in zebra finches, we showed large-scale behavior-dependent activity in both juvenile and adult individuals. MINI2P-II opens the door to multi-region 2P imaging across species and developmental stages in freely moving animals.

piezas.resumenOriginal: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is implicated in many cognitive tasks, including working memory, reward-based decision-making, executive control, and metacognition. This exploratory analysis investigated whether individual expression of PFC cortical thickness and surface area covariance components is associated with cognitive task performance. The sample comprised Human Connectome Project (HCP) MRI data from 743 healthy adults (age 22–36+). Oblimin-rotated principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to residualized thickness and surface area for 22 PFC regions, controlling for age, sex, and ICV. Component scores were entered as predictors in separate regression models for the Flanker Age-Adjusted Score (inhibitory control), the Gambling RT Difference (RT for the same “larger” guess in reward minus punishment blocks), and 2-Back median RT (working memory speed). Parallel analysis favored two thickness components; a prespecified three-component solution (Global/Lateral PFC, RC1; Orbitofrontal, RC2; Anterior Cingulate, RC3; 53.7% of variance) was retained by decision, and RC1 and RC2 were only moderately stable across bootstrap resamples. RC1 was nominally associated with lower Flanker scores (β = −0.103, p = 0.027), opposite to the predicted direction, and RC2 with a smaller Gambling RT Difference (β = −0.103, p = 0.025); neither survived false discovery rate (FDR) correction (q = 0.054). In uncorrected models added at review, whole-cortex mean thickness alone robustly predicted Flanker scores but not the Gambling RT Difference; neither component association survived regressing mean thickness out before PCA. In surface area analyses, greater orbitofrontal surface area (AC2) was associated with faster 2-Back RT (β = −0.125, p = 0.003; q = 0.032 across 12 surface area tests and 0.064 across all 24 component tests), not explained by a speed-accuracy tradeoff. This unpredicted association persisted in most sensitivity analyses but was attenuated and non-significant when total surface area was regressed out before PCA (β = −0.065, p = 0.078). In conclusion, no prefrontal-specific association was robust. Global cortical thickness accounts for the Flanker association more parsimoniously, the Gambling RT Difference association was not robust under either account, and the orbitofrontal surface area association could not be separated from global surface area; all associations require replication.

destilado.texto: ¿Puede la forma de la corteza prefrontal predecir la rapidez en tareas de memoria? Un análisis de resonancia magnética del Human Connectome Project halló que mayor superficie orbitofrontal se relaciona con tiempos más cortos en la prueba 2‑Back, aunque la asociación no supera la corrección por falsos descubrimientos. ¿Qué sigue?

piezas.titulo: Opening the Black Box of Ayres Sensory Integration<sup>®</sup>: Clarifying Mechanisms of Change from Treatment Theory to Participation.
piezas.resumenOriginal: Ayres Sensory Integration ® (ASI) remains one of the most widely used and debated intervention approaches in occupational therapy and related disciplines. Recent advances in rehabilitation treatment specification and reporting frameworks, including the Rehabilitation Treatment Specification System (RTSS) and the Reporting Guideline for Intervention Description in Rehabilitation (GUIDE-Rehab), emphasize the need for precise articulation of treatment ingredients, mechanisms of action, and targets. However, interventions grounded in neurodevelopmental theories, such as Ayres' theory of sensory integration, are complex, and may present challenges when interpreted within linear causal models. This paper argues that ASI theory is best understood as a treatment theory targeting proximal sensory-motor capacities, while participation-level outcomes may be more comprehensively explained through an enablement framework. Integrating this perspective with data-driven decision making (DDDM) clarifies longstanding ambiguities in the ASI literature and strengthens intervention specification, evaluation, and interpretation.

piezas.titulo: Lifestyle Documentation in Therapy Evaluations for Autistic Children: A Lexicon-Based Analysis of Electronic Health Records.
piezas.resumenOriginal: BackgroundWhole person health (WPH) is a multidimensional construct encompassing, physical, and mental health along with relational constructs such as social health that are deeply tied to well-being. Autistic individuals report an overall lower quality of life, but the extent to which these issues are addressed during therapy evaluations has not been examined systematically.MethodologyIn this retrospective, cross-sectional study, we employ a rule-based NLP/lexicon-based approach to examine the areas of focus of therapy evaluations documented by occupational therapy, physical therapy (PT), and speech-language pathology (SLP) professionals. Using electronic health records for children aged 2 to 18 diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (n = 5619 evaluation reports of n = 2021 unique patients), we classified health records based on the domains addressed.ResultsAcross notes, nutrition had the highest average degree of documentation ( M = 2.14), compared to activity ( M = 0.91), followed by wellness ( M = 0.66), and sleep ( M = 0.39). In occupational therapy, wellness was the most common (77.62% of notes), followed by physical activity (76.49% of notes), nutrition management (73.33% of notes), and sleep (34.97% of notes). The overall area under the curve (AUC) from the receiver operating characteristic analysis is 0.89.ConclusionsWhile it is encouraging that most evaluations addressed nutrition or physical activity, the near absence of attention to sleep represents a critical gap in care. Given sleep's foundational role in overall health and daily functioning, its omission is particularly concerning. Occupational therapists and interdisciplinary rehabilitation teams should more deliberately integrate WPH frameworks into their evaluations.

piezas.titulo: Airbnb Cuts Recommendation Staleness from 2 Days to Seconds with Chronon
piezas.resumenOriginal: Airbnb extended its Chronon feature platform with Push Mode and Near Real-Time Model Transform to update sequence-based recommendation embeddings within seconds. The architecture reduced embedding staleness from nearly two days to under a minute and improved offline NDCG by 1.67%, while online testing increased uncancelled bookings by approximately one-third of a percent. By Leela Kumili

destilado.texto: ¿Puede una plataforma actualizar sus recomendaciones en segundos? Airbnb lanzó el modo Push y la transformación de modelo casi en tiempo real en Chronon, reduciendo la obsolescencia de los embeddings de casi dos días a menos de un minuto. El cambio elevó reservas sin cancelación en casi un tercio de por ciento.
